title: Two-Batch Arm Elimination for Best-Arm Identification with Heterogeneous Known Variances
banked_reason: D0.5.G: exact proportional top-m frontier is sound and complete, but unrestricted first-stage and branch-specific allocation optimality remains open; paper_score_ceiling 6.7 < 7.4 field floor.
gap_reasons: The exact exponent, matching worst-instance witnesses, timing optimum, and survivor-count optimization are proved only for the proportional top-m two-batch family relative to the variance-aware GNA static comparator; optimality over unrestricted first-stage and branch-specific allocations remains open.
The finite-T result is only a mean-dependent union-bound certificate, not finite-sample dominance or a guarantee computable from known variances alone.

The narrow known-Gaussian setting, absence of practical evaluation, and unresolved unrestricted-design saddle keep the package below flagship level and constrain its leading-econometrics-journal score.
proof_attempt_summary: The run proved the exact finite-branch exponent and rounding invariance for proportional top-m two-batch designs, matching best-exclusion and terminal witnesses, optimal timing and survivor count, and the common-variance √K elbow with gain tending to two. The field-tier claim collapsed at unrestricted-design optimality: arbitrary first-stage and branch-specific allocations destroy the fixed projection geometry and scalar survivor-expansion converse. What remains is a new allocation-uniform saddle certificate or an exact superior nonproportional construction, rather than a bounded repair of the completed derivation.
tldr: For every \(K\ge3\) and every known finite positive Gaussian variance vector, a fully specified proportional two-batch rule can retain any top \(m\in\{2,\ldots,K-1\}\) first-batch arms and reallocate the remaining budget proportionally among them. The exact Gaussian exponent is a finite minimum over \(\binom{K-1}{m}\) best-exclusion and \((m-1)\binom{K-1}{m-1}\) terminal branches. Weighted projections and separated matching witnesses give \(L_m(\rho)=\min\{\rho C_m,1+(1-\rho)\eta_{K-m}\}\), the unique timing \(\rho_m^\star=(1+\eta_{K-m})/(C_m+\eta_{K-m})\), and gain \(G_m>1\). Enumerating \(m\) yields the certified design \(G_{\mathrm{multi}}=\max_m G_m\); in the common-variance subclass its optimal survivor count is of order \(\sqrt K\) and the gain tends to two. The connection to Imbens, Qin, and Wager is the batched-arm-elimination motif; literal distributional and comparator overlap is the common-variance subclass.
gap: The closest same-design result, Imbens, Qin, and Wager’s common-variance batched arm-elimination theorem, gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. It does not supply the heteroskedastic weighted branch contraction, exact terminal-branch equality, or dominance over Kato’s variance-aware equal-gap maximin allocation.
fill: The project derives the weighted heteroskedastic contraction and exact coupled terminal-branch equality, then reduces the worst best-elimination event to \(K\) one-dimensional piecewise-quadratic calculations, proves a whole-positive-orthant gain, and certifies the exact maximin timing within the proportional family.
